readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: “What are you going to do about it?” (Introduction, end)
readings.challenge: Follow an argument about causes that leans on quoted official reports.
readings.focus: Whether drink or housing explains poverty, and who Riis thinks must pay for the remedy.
readings.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this study of the city’s tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. The Introduction has described the “boundary line” between rich and poor in New York and promised to show how the tenements grew. William M. Tweed, boss of the Tammany Hall political machine, was said to have answered charges of fraud in 1871 with “What are you going to do about it?” The upas-tree was a legendary tree said to poison everything near it. Model-housing reformers of the time promised investors “philanthropy and five per cent.,” a modest but steady return.

excerpt.locator: Introduction, the last two paragraphs with Riis’s two notes; opens “What are you going to do about it? is the question of to-day. It was asked once of our…”; closes “…of God be understood by those who have been nurtured in sight only of the greed of man?"”.

questions.prompt: Riis takes his opening question from “a band of political cutthroats.” Why begin the remedy with a corrupt politician’s taunt, and how does the note about Tweed sharpen it?
facilitatorNotes: The taunt becomes the question the city must now answer about its tenements. The note that Tweed “was born and bred in a Fourth Ward tenement” makes the slums the source of the corruption that once defied the law, and hints that a larger “appeal for justice” is coming. Some readers will find the warning more alarmist than the evidence supports.
evidence: What are you going to do about it? is the question of to-day.
Tweed was born and bred in a Fourth Ward tenement.

questions.prompt: Riis sets two explanations of poverty side by side. What evidence does he give for drunkenness as the cause, and what for housing? Which does he favor?
facilitatorNotes: One official report blames drink for forty per cent. of the distress; an earlier committee found that living conditions are “the prolific parents” of habits and morals, and proposed preventing drunkenness by giving every man a decent home. Riis favors housing, treating drink as an effect. A skeptic will note that he chose which reports to quote.
evidence: Forty per cent. of the distress among the poor, said a recent official report, is due to drunkenness.
certain conditions and associations of human life and habitation are the prolific parents of corresponding habits and morals

questions.prompt: What does the quoted sanitary inquiry reveal about who owned the tenements and how they were run? Why does Riis stress the words “generally a speculation”?
facilitatorNotes: Most were held by owners who ran them as a business at a return that “very rarely fell below fifteen per cent.” and often passed thirty (the note reports forty as a fair average and instances of a hundred and over); repairs were refused and the agent’s rule was rent in advance or eviction. Stressing “speculation” makes housing a gamble on the poor rather than a service to them.
evidence: generally a speculation
Collect the rent in advance, or, failing, eject the occupants.

questions.prompt: Riis says “The greed of capital that wrought the evil must itself undo it.” Why does he think neither law nor charity can do it, and how does the Brooklyn builder’s question move the argument from money to religion?
facilitatorNotes: Employers must build decent homes and owners must accept a fair return instead of “good property” in the heartless sense. The last paragraph asks churches how they can reach people raised “in sight only of the greed of man”: the economic remedy is also a moral one. Students may debate whether a private, modest-profit solution could ever be enough.
evidence: The greed of capital that wrought the evil must itself undo it
How shall the love of God be understood by those who have been nurtured in sight only of the greed of man?

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: worse was to follow (Chapter I, end)
readings.challenge: Weigh statistics, quoted reports, and three eyewitness cases as kinds of evidence.
readings.focus: How the business of subletting produced the slums, and how Riis makes the past present.
readings.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this study of the city’s tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Chapter I tells how the old houses of New York’s merchants, abandoned for uptown, were divided room by room for the poor: the first tenements. Gotham Court was a notorious tenement block. Riis’s notes are numbered as in the transcription. Note 4 belongs to a floor plan printed beside this page, “Tenement of 1863, for twelve families on each flat,” which is not reproduced here.
readings.contentNote: Riis mentions a young couple who poisoned themselves because they were “tired,” and calls a family “colored,” the period term.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Genesis of the Tenement,” from the coming of the middleman to the end of the chapter, with notes 3–5; opens “Worse was to follow. It was "soon perceived by estate owners and agents of property that…”; closes “…twenty stables, rented for dwellings at $15 a year each; cost of the whole $600."]”.

questions.prompt: According to the first paragraph, what changed when the middleman appeared? Trace the chain from his arrival to the death rates Riis cites.
facilitatorNotes: Owners realized that houses could be turned into “barracks” and rented to middlemen who sublet by the room; with these irresponsible landlords began the building of blocks like Gotham Court, where cholera killed one hundred and ninety-five per thousand and the city’s whole death rate rose. Riis links a business arrangement to a body count.
evidence: With the appearance of the middleman, wholly irresponsible, and utterly reckless and unrestrained
the tenants died at the rate of one hundred and ninety-five to the thousand of population

questions.prompt: Riis piles up figures: 290,000 to the square mile, Old London’s 175,816, “China not excluded.” What do the numbers do that description cannot, and where does he leave numbers for a single picture?
facilitatorNotes: The comparisons make the crowding unprecedented on a world scale. Then he narrows to “one room 12 × 12” holding twenty people and a cellar where hogs were fed, details a reader can see. His dry closing line, that the rent has held up “though the hog at least has been eliminated,” turns the history into an accusation about the present.
evidence: it was packed at the rate of 290,000 to the square mile
one room 12 × 12 with five families living in it
though the hog at least has been eliminated

questions.prompt: “Lest anybody flatter himself” introduces three “very recent instances.” What does each case show, and why does Riis add that the burned house’s owner “considered himself especially entitled to be pitied”?
facilitatorNotes: The fire shows rent far beyond value and an owner who sees only his loss; the couple’s suicide shows exhaustion that needed no explanation once Riis saw their attic; the family’s room was too small to photograph. The remark about the owner is irony aimed at a reader who might sympathize with property first.
evidence: He evidently considered himself especially entitled to be pitied for losing such valuable property.
There was no other explanation, and none was needed when I stood in the room in which they had lived.

questions.prompt: The chapter ends on a fact from the city directory. What is the irony of placing the “American Society for the Promotion of Education in Africa” after the juvenile crime of New York?
facilitatorNotes: The city had no Children’s Aid Society yet for its own vagrant children, but it had a society to educate Africans: charity looked abroad while its own streets filled with neglected children. Some readers may also hear a dismissive tone toward the African cause itself; the sentence works chiefly as a rebuke to misplaced benevolence.
evidence: The Children's Aid Society and kindred philanthropic organizations were yet unborn
American Society for the Promotion of Education in Africa

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: the saw in the dark bedrooms (Chapter II, opening)
readings.challenge: Test the analogies a reformer uses to explain why reform keeps falling behind.
readings.focus: The first tenement laws, the resistance to them, and the fear behind them.
readings.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this study of the city’s tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Chapter I ended in the 1840s and 1850s with the tenements crowded and their children on the streets. New York’s Board of Health and the Tenement-House Act of 1867, the city’s first housing law, came after the Civil War. Sanitarians were public-health reformers. Nemesis is the Greek goddess of retribution; a proletariat is a propertyless working class.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “The Awakening,” the first two paragraphs; opens “The dread of advancing cholera, with the guilty knowledge of the harvest field that…”; closes “…of the poor," as the Council of Hygiene mildly put it, has of avenging itself.”.

questions.prompt: What finally “pricked the conscience of the community into action”? What does this suggest about why reform came when it did?
facilitatorNotes: The dread of cholera, with the “guilty knowledge” of where it would strike. Reform followed fear for the whole city, not only pity for the poor. Readers can debate whether self-interest makes the reform less admirable or simply more likely.
evidence: The dread of advancing cholera
pricked the conscience of the community into action

questions.prompt: Who opposed the cutting of forty-six thousand windows, and why does Riis say their objection was, “curiously enough,” the same?
facilitatorNotes: Owners saw only expense; tenants, sunk “to the level of their surroundings,” resisted too. Both called inspection an infringement of personal rights. Riis is hard on the tenants here, treating resignation as a moral failing; students can ask whether a generation of “unavailing protest” is a better explanation.
evidence: owner and tenant alike considered official interference an infringement of personal rights
had sunk, after a generation of unavailing protest, to the level of their surroundings

questions.prompt: “The tenements had bred their Nemesis.” Who is the Nemesis, and what is Riis warning his readers about?
facilitatorNotes: A class of the poor “ready and able to avenge the wrongs” done to them, already costly in jails and charities. The warning appeals to the comfortable reader’s fear of disorder. Some readers find it a fair forecast; others find it a frightening image of the poor that sits uneasily with Riis’s sympathy.
evidence: The tenements had bred their Nemesis, a proletariat ready and able to avenge the wrongs of their crowds.

questions.prompt: In the second paragraph Riis compares the evil to a fire and to “one bad boy in a schoolroom.” What do these analogies explain well, and what do they hide?
facilitatorNotes: The fire explains why reformers chasing old cases fall behind: an evil that spreads must be headed off. The schoolroom image explains how the worst houses drag neighbors down. Both make the slum a force of nature or a naughty child and can hide the builders’ choices, though Riis himself notes that the new tenements were planned as badly as the old.
evidence: like a fire, it could only be headed off, not chased, with success
just as one bad boy in a schoolroom will spoil the whole class

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: the mixed crowd (Chapter III, part 1)
readings.challenge: Separate Riis’s environmental argument from his generalizations about nationalities.
readings.focus: Who lives in the tenements, and how Riis sorts the poor.
readings.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this study of the city’s tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Chapter III surveys the immigrant groups crowded into lower Manhattan in 1890. Riis, himself an immigrant, writes with the confident generalizations about “races” and nationalities common in his time. Job advertisements earlier in the century often said “No Irish need apply.” “Celtic” means Irish. Riis renders the Sicilian tenant’s report of his landlord in mock dialect.
readings.contentNote: Riis’s sweeping generalizations about the Irish and Italians, his mock dialect, and terms such as “Chinaman” and “low Irish” are the source’s; the questions ask readers to test them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “The Mixed Crowd,” from the Fourth Ward alley’s tenants through the German rag-pickers, with note 6; opens “When once I asked the agent of a notorious Fourth Ward alley how many people might be…”; closes “…colony moved out there in a body. There need be no doubt about their thriving there.]”.

questions.prompt: “Where have they gone to, the old inhabitants?” How do the old man’s answer and Riis’s own describe lower New York?
facilitatorNotes: No “distinctively American community” exists among the tenements; the old stock went west, to war, or to the grave. The man who misses the days of “no Irish need apply” is gently mocked: he cannot say where his own people went.
evidence: The one thing you shall vainly ask for in the chief city of America is a distinctively American community.
I don't see them 'round here.

questions.prompt: Explain the image of “whiskey and water in one glass.” What does it predict, and what attitude toward the newcomers does it carry?
facilitatorNotes: The groups mix into one population in which the Irish flavor prevails, as the next sentences explain: the Irish run the politics and own the houses. The joke depends on a stereotype of Irish drinking, and calling the mass “queer” and “heterogeneous” shows Riis’s distance from it. Readers can discuss whether the image is affectionate or contemptuous.
evidence: like whiskey and water in one glass, and with the like result: final union and a prevailing taint of whiskey

questions.prompt: After the story of the Irish landlord, Riis writes “In justice to the Irish landlord.” What is his defense, and does it excuse the landlord?
facilitatorNotes: The landlord learned his methods from the tenement system itself, “like an apt pupil”; only his frankness shocks. This is Riis’s environmental argument, but in the same paragraph he speaks of Irish character and of a “sediment” of “low Irish,” mixing structural and ethnic explanations. Students may decide that it explains without excusing.
evidence: like an apt pupil he was merely showing forth the result of the schooling he had received
It is only his frankness that shocks.

questions.prompt: How does Riis distinguish the “truly poor” from “the sediment of the slums”? What does the note on the German rag-pickers prove, and what does it leave unproved?
facilitatorNotes: Wage-earners are poor because rents are high and homes are bad; the “sediment” is a lasting moral residue that menaces the rest. The note shows one colony that saved and moved west together, evidence that people rise when they can. It does not show that the “sediment” is different in kind; that remains Riis’s judgment.
evidence: They are truly poor for having no better homes
the steadier growth of the sediment of the slums and its constant menace
The thrifty Germans saved up money during years of hard work in squalor

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: a map in many colors (Chapter III, part 2)
readings.challenge: Read a vivid extended metaphor for the assumptions built into it.
readings.focus: Riis’s map of nationalities: what it shows, and what it says about its maker.
readings.context: Recap: Riis has found no “distinctively American community” among the tenements, only a mass of nationalities, and has argued that wage-earners are poor because they cannot find better homes, while a “sediment” sinks to the bottom. “Teuton” means German, and “Dutchman” was slang for a German. “Coolie” was a term for a low-paid Asian laborer. In the draft riots of July 1863, mobs attacked and killed Black New Yorkers. “Djumala” is the Finnish word for God.
readings.contentNote: This passage is built from ethnic and racial stereotypes, including antisemitic ones, and describes Italians “pursuing” Black New Yorkers in images of war; “Chinaman,” “coolie,” “negro” and “the Arab tribe” are the source’s terms. The discussion examines them as evidence of Riis’s assumptions.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “The Mixed Crowd,” from the Italian scavenger to the end of the chapter; opens “The Italian scavenger of our time is fast graduating into exclusive control of the corner…”; closes “…as he can save up money enough, he gets out and never crosses the threshold of one again.”.

questions.prompt: Riis begins by insisting the immigrant “has been unjustly blamed.” What is his evidence that newcomers rise when given “half a chance”?
facilitatorNotes: The Italian scavenger moves to fruit-stands, the Irish hod-carrier’s son becomes a bricklayer or an Alderman, the Chinese laborer runs laundries. The bad homes are not chosen but imposed. Students may notice that his examples are themselves narrow ethnic trades.
evidence: given half a chance, might be reasonably expected to make the most of it
for the bad result he has been unjustly blamed

questions.prompt: Describe the imagined map. What does the metaphor let Riis do, and what does a map of colors hide about the people it shows?
facilitatorNotes: It gives the reader an overview of a confusing city: green Irish, blue Germans, Italian red, and “an extraordinary crazy-quilt.” It also turns people into blocks of color that advance and retreat, erasing individuals and the landlords and employers who decide where people can live.
evidence: A map of the city, colored to designate nationalities
an extraordinary crazy-quilt

questions.prompt: Find the language of war in the account of Italian and Black New Yorkers (“onset,” “foe,” “main body,” “on the march”). What story do these words tell, and what does Riis pass over about why Black families moved?
facilitatorNotes: Migration becomes a campaign of conquest, with Black residents retreating before Italians. Riis mentions in passing that the draft riots “drove the negroes out” of Cherry Street and the Five Points, but not that this was mob violence; the war metaphor makes displacement sound natural. Some readers find the metaphor merely vivid; others find it dehumanizing.
evidence: still pursued by the Italian foe, is on the march yet
when the draft-riots drove the negroes out of reach of Cherry Street and the Five Points

questions.prompt: In the closing ranking, who “makes the most of life thus mortgaged,” and on what evidence? Test one of Riis’s judgments against his own argument about “half a chance.”
facilitatorNotes: He awards “the palm” to the Germans, who keep a home and leave the tenement as soon as they can, and declares that the Italian and the poor Jew rise “only by compulsion” and the Chinese “not at all.” These are assertions without evidence, and they contradict his claim two paragraphs earlier that circumstances, not character, explain failure. Students may note that the northern European most like Riis himself comes out best.
evidence: the palm must be unhesitatingly awarded the Teuton
The Italian and the poor Jew rise only by compulsion.
The Chinaman does not rise at all

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: Cherry Street and Blind Man’s Alley (Chapter IV)
readings.challenge: Notice how a guided tour positions the reader as a visitor.
readings.focus: Decayed grandeur, a blind landlord of blind tenants, and Riis’s mixed sympathies.
readings.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this study of the city’s tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Chapter IV is a walking tour of the old Fourth Ward, under the Brooklyn Bridge, where the first tenements were built; Riis writes “we” and “us” as if leading the reader. The Knickerbocker houses were the homes of old Dutch-descended families; Cherry Hill was once fashionable. A truant officer enforced school attendance. Calvary is a Catholic cemetery.
readings.contentNote: Riis jokes about immigrants’ large families, and a landlord says his blind tenants “are not fit to live in a nice house.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Down Town Back-Alleys,” from the opening through the blind landlord’s appeal; opens “Down below Chatham Square, in the old Fourth Ward, where the cradle of the tenement…”; closes “…away and did not return. Some remained, however, and the name has clung to the place.”.

questions.prompt: “There is nothing to be afraid of,” Riis assures his reader. What kind of visitor does he imagine, and what joke does he make at the native-born reader’s expense?
facilitatorNotes: A sober stranger who minds his own business; the only danger is being taken for a truant officer. The joke about “the American stock” dying out “for want of children” teases readers anxious about immigrant birth rates, and the swarming children make the point. Some will hear the joke as sharing that anxiety rather than mocking it.
evidence: provided he knows how to mind his own business and is sober
the American stock is dying out for want of children

questions.prompt: How does Riis use one old Knickerbocker house to tell a history? Find the details that set past and present against each other.
facilitatorNotes: Broad steps, dormers and a handsome cornice against rotting columns, boarded fireplaces and a “dark and nameless alley” where a gateway once led to a garden by a stream. The house is given a “querulous second childhood,” and Riis imagines its “glowing firesides.” The contrast blames the heedless builders of the barracks around it.
evidence: the old Knickerbocker houses linger like ghosts of a departed day
what glowing firesides, what happy children may it once have owned?
but to a dark and nameless alley

questions.prompt: Who is “Old Dan” Murphy, and what is the irony of his last years? What does his speech to the Board of Health reveal?
facilitatorNotes: He made a fortune from the alley of blind beggars and went blind himself, sharing the hardship he refused to relieve. His appeal moves from pathos (the grave, the monument) to rage at being “skinned,” and to contempt for his tenants.
evidence: only to grow blind himself in extreme old age
These people are not fit to live in a nice house.

questions.prompt: Riis says “Mr. Murphy had gauged his tenants correctly,” since many left after the cleaning. Does Riis agree that they were “not fit to live in a nice house”? Weigh the evidence.
facilitatorNotes: The text allows two readings. Riis may mean only that the tenants, attached to their old home, would not stay in a changed one; or he may half concede Murphy’s contempt. He also finds the old man’s distrust of builders “downright amusing.” The ambiguity is typical of Riis’s mix of sympathy and condescension.
evidence: The result showed that Mr. Murphy had gauged his tenants correctly.
The cleaning up process apparently destroyed the home-feeling of the alley

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: the Dirty Spoon and Gotham Court (Chapter IV)
readings.challenge: Read the reporter’s own blunder and jokes as part of his evidence.
readings.focus: Filth beyond cleaning, charity that returns to the landlord, and a model tenement gone wrong.
readings.context: Recap: Riis has led the reader from the Brooklyn Bridge into Cherry Street and Blind Man’s Alley, whose blind landlord grew rich from it and fought the Board of Health’s order to clean it up. A flash-light picture used a flash of burning magnesium powder; Riis was a pioneer of flash photography in the slums. The “Out-door Poor” received city relief at home. A King’s Daughter belonged to a Christian women’s charitable order. The Swamp Angels were a gang that used the sewers.
readings.contentNote: Riis renders a Chinese man’s and an old woman’s speech in mock dialect and uses “Chinaman”; he says the Italians seek, “according to their wont, the lowest level.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Down Town Back-Alleys,” from the fire in the Dirty Spoon through the history of Gotham Court; opens “Some idea of what is meant by a sanitary "cleaning up" in these slums may be gained from…”; closes “…must have been congenial. Probably "Jimmy" himself fitted into the landscape.”.

questions.prompt: Retell the story of the fire Riis set with his flash. What does the policeman’s joke about the “Dirty Spoon” reveal, and why does Riis end with “those who insure houses”?
facilitatorNotes: Riis admits his own clumsiness and his fear for five blind people up a rickety stair. The policeman laughs: the walls are so filthy that fire smothers. The closing irony is that dirt protects the insurers’ risk, not the tenants; a “cleaning up” here has barely begun. Readers may also notice the photographer as an intruder who endangered his subjects.
evidence: With unpractised hands I managed to set fire to the house.
The dirt was so thick on the walls, it smothered the fire!
work together for the good of those who insure houses

questions.prompt: What is the blind beggars’ “pay-day,” and how does Riis mix sympathy with judgment in describing it?
facilitatorNotes: Once a year the city distributes its allowance to the poor blind, “in half-hearted recognition” of its failure to provide otherwise; the alley sings and fiddles. The last sentence turns the celebration: much of the money goes to the landlord.
evidence: in half-hearted recognition of its failure to otherwise provide for them
Even the blind landlord rejoices, for much of the money goes into his coffers.

questions.prompt: Describe the plan of Gotham Court. Why does Riis stress that it was built “by a benevolent Quaker for the express purpose of rescuing the poor”?
facilitatorNotes: Two rows of five-story tenements back to back, with barred openings so tenants can see but not reach each other, between two alleys. A building meant to rescue became a place where 61 of 138 children died within three years. The history warns that good intentions without good design and management can fail.
evidence: with barred openings in the dividing wall, so that the tenants may see but cannot get at each other from the stairs
was originally built (in 1851) by a benevolent Quaker for the express purpose of rescuing the poor people

questions.prompt: Riis reports several explanations for the iron bars and the policeman. What is the joke, and is Riis’s own explanation better supported?
facilitatorNotes: The Irish blame two German families; a Chinese passer-by blames the Irish; Riis blames “the mixed character” of Irish and Italian tenants. Everyone blames another group, Riis included, and none offers evidence. The mock dialect for the Chinese man adds ridicule; students can ask what the joke shows about the city and about the writer.
evidence: The mixed character of the population, by this time about equally divided between the Celtic and the Italian stock, accounts for the iron bars and the policeman.
made trouble all the time

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: the Quaker’s wall and the sunless alley (Chapter IV)
readings.challenge: Track the moments where a reporter’s even tone breaks into outrage.
readings.focus: Spite, violence, and what light and air are worth to an owner.
readings.context: Recap: on his tour of the Fourth Ward Riis has shown Blind Man’s Alley and Gotham Court, a model tenement built by a Quaker in 1851 that became notorious for disease and crime. “Rushing the growler” or a “can racket” meant sending a pail out for beer; the excise law regulated liquor. “The Island” was Blackwell’s Island and its prison; Hell Gate is a narrow strait of the East River. “The wickedest man in New York” was a dance-hall keeper of the 1860s.
readings.contentNote: A man is killed in a brawl over beer, and another falls from a roof during a police “fusillade.”

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Down Town Back-Alleys,” from the Quaker’s revenge through the Roosevelt Street alley; opens “Half-way back from the street in this latter alley is a tenement, facing the main…”; closes “…built of and upon the successful assertion of the truth that all men are created equal.”.

questions.prompt: Tell the story of the Quaker’s wall. Why does Riis call it “a curious monument to a Quaker’s revenge”?
facilitatorNotes: Knocked down by Alderman Mullins, the Quaker answered with a blank wall in front of Mullins’s windows; the building behind it could not even be let. The quiet “I will pay thee” clashes with Quaker pacifism, and the cost fell on thousands of tenants who never quarreled with anyone.
evidence: a living illustration of the power of hate to perpetuate its bitter fruit beyond the grave
I will pay thee for that, friend Alderman

questions.prompt: “What, indeed, was there to say?” How do the wake and the police “fusillade” explain that closing question?
facilitatorNotes: A man is cut to pieces over beer, and nobody makes a fuss; the police, called to keep the peace, open fire and a man falls from a roof, and only the usual wake follows. Violence is so ordinary that it produces no news. The question may voice the neighborhood’s resignation, the press’s indifference, or Riis’s own bitterness.
evidence: It is nothing unusual on Cherry Street
There was the usual wake and nothing more was heard of it.

questions.prompt: Read the description of the Roosevelt Street alley. Where does Riis break his reporter’s tone, and what does the English doctor’s experiment add to his case?
facilitatorNotes: “God help us for pitiful mockery!” breaks in where a five-story house takes its light from a slit between walls the sun never reaches. The experiment in soldiers’ barracks gives scientific weight: mortality doubled on the sunless side. Riis then turns the evidence into a question of who is worth protecting.
evidence: God help us for pitiful mockery!
found that on the side that was shut off altogether from the sun the mortality was one hundred per cent. greater

questions.prompt: The paragraph ends with “the successful assertion of the truth that all men are created equal.” How does the comparison with the horse lead there, and whom is Riis attacking?
facilitatorNotes: Soldiers have “a fixed value”; the laborers have none, and the employer values his cart-horse above the man who loads it, which both owner and man know. The employer’s prosperity rests on a nation founded on equality: the line is savage irony. A few readers may hear sincere faith that equality made his success possible; the context makes the irony hard to miss.
evidence: The horse that pulls the dirt-cart one of these laborers loads and unloads is of ever so much more account
built of and upon the successful assertion of the truth that all men are created equal

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: from Madison Street to “The Ship” (Chapter IV)
readings.challenge: Separate reported fact from generalization in a passage that mixes sympathy and prejudice.
readings.focus: What separates rich from poor, a builder’s new front, and Riis’s view of Jewish newcomers.
readings.context: Recap: Riis’s walk through the Fourth Ward has passed Gotham Court, the Quaker’s spite wall, and an alley the sun never reaches, which he set against an employer who values his horse above his workmen. Satyrs are the leering half-goat figures of Greek myth. “Hebrews” and “Israelite” were period terms for Jews, and “Jewtown” the name then used for the Jewish quarter of the Lower East Side.
readings.contentNote: A tenement fire kills women and children. The paragraph on Jewish newcomers uses antisemitic stereotypes about money and property; the questions ask readers to examine them.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Down Town Back-Alleys,” from the Madison Street fire to “The Ship” in Hamilton Street; opens “With what a shock did the story of yonder Madison Street alley come home to New Yorkers…”; closes “…there are no dives there, nothing worse than the ubiquitous saloon and tough tenements.”.

questions.prompt: What happened in the Madison Street alley, and what does Riis conclude from the “wonderfully heroic rescues”?
facilitatorNotes: A fire after the men left for work killed about ten women and children; the fire-escapes could not be reached. The neighbors’ heroism shows that the poor are no different in kind from the rich: the gap “is, after all, perhaps but a tenement.” Then he asks whose making that gap is.
evidence: There were fire-escapes, yes! but so placed that they could not be reached.
the gap that separates the man with the patched coat from his wealthy neighbor is, after all, perhaps but a tenement

questions.prompt: Explain the satyrs’ heads. What does Riis suggest about the builder by asking whether their leer is “an introspective grin”?
facilitatorNotes: The new tenement will be called an apartment house and gets a carved brown-stone front, next to houses the same respectable builder ran until they were condemned. The leering stone faces seem to mock the builder, or to grin at their own pretense. The last line echoes the “reformed” thief earlier: the builder too “may have reformed.”
evidence: They are carving satyrs' heads in the stone
Is it only in our fancy that the sardonic leer on the stone faces seems to list that way?
He too may have reformed.

questions.prompt: In the paragraph on Penitentiary Row, separate the facts Riis reports from the generalizations he draws. Which are stereotypes, and how do they sit beside his mockery of the old sign over the door?
facilitatorNotes: Facts: Jewish pedlars and tailors have filled the block, are buying old houses and building new ones, and an old sign said “No pedlars allowed.” Generalizations: that “the Jew runs to real estate,” pockets abuse “with the rent,” and patiently takes his persecutors’ property, an old antisemitic picture of Jewish money. Riis mocks the prejudice of the sign and repeats a prejudice himself. Students may read him as admiring, hostile, or both.
evidence: The Jew runs to real estate as soon as he can save up enough for a deposit
He pockets them quietly with the rent and bides his time.

questions.prompt: Why might Riis place the father and son on the ash-cart, “a pleasure party,” here?
facilitatorNotes: After fires, spite walls and landlords, a moment of pride and joy restores the people as people; the comparison with “the avenue” claims the same happiness for them. Some readers find the scene condescending (“brown-legged boy”); others find it a needed reminder that the tour is about lives, not only buildings.
evidence: Here comes a pleasure party, as gay as any on the avenue, though the carry-all is an ash-cart.
How proud and happy they both look up there on their perch!

readings.title: How the Other Half Lives: “Is life worth living?” (Chapter IV, end)
readings.challenge: Hear sarcasm aimed at an argument rather than at its victims.
readings.focus: Two families, a death, and the comfortable theory that the poor do not feel it.
readings.context: Jacob A. Riis (1849–1914), a Danish immigrant who became a New York police reporter, published this study of the city’s tenement housing in 1890, illustrated with his own photographs. Chapter IV has walked the reader through the alleys of the Fourth and Seventh Wards and into a Cherry Street tenement where a baby died in a dark bedroom. “Is life worth living?” was a much-debated question of the 1880s. The Association for Improving the Condition of the Poor was a New York charity; consumption is tuberculosis.
readings.contentNote: A mother takes her own life by jumping from a window; the passage discusses despair and suicide.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Down Town Back-Alleys,” the last two paragraphs; opens “What sort of an answer, think you, would come from these tenements to the question "Is…”; closes “…as the refuge from every trouble, and shapes its practice according to the discovery.”.

questions.prompt: What answer do the two cases give to the question “Is life worth living?”
facilitatorNotes: A seaman with consumption cannot feed or warm his children in a garret open to the winter, the baby swinging in a shawl from the rafters; a mother in a family of nine in two rooms throws herself from the window. The tenements answer by deaths and despair, though Riis lets the cases speak rather than state it.
evidence: the baby was swung in an old shawl attached to the rafters by cords by way of a hammock
That day the mother had thrown herself out of the window

questions.prompt: Why does Riis insist that the second case was “typical enough to escape that reproach”? What makes the German family typical rather than exceptional?
facilitatorNotes: They are honest, hard-working, neat, with one breadwinner whose week’s wages do not cover the month’s rent: the respectable poor, not the “vicious.” If such people break, the cause is the housing and wages, not character. Students can note that Riis’s argument again depends on the family being “deserving.”
evidence: honest, hard-working Germans, scrupulously neat, but poor
more than a week's wages for the husband and father

questions.prompt: Who is Riis’s “optimistic friend,” and how does Riis take apart his “philosophy of the slums”?
facilitatorNotes: Someone who believes the tenement poor “do not take it as hard” and that life there is bearable. Riis lets the theory refute itself (it cannot explain the dead woman) and ends by naming the slum’s real philosophy: the saloon as refuge.
evidence: Philosophy, according to my optimistic friend, naturally inhabits the tenements.
He has never found time to explain how the fact fits into his general theory that life is not unbearable in the tenements.

questions.prompt: Right after the woman’s death Riis tells of four families keeping house in the four corners of one room. Is the humor appropriate?
facilitatorNotes: “No doubt she was wrong in not taking life philosophically” is sarcasm aimed at the optimist, and the four-family anecdote is a deadpan example of the “philosophy” he mocks. Some readers find the turn jarring after a suicide; others think the bitterness is the point.
evidence: No doubt she was wrong in not taking life philosophically
They got along well enough together until one of the families took a boarder and made trouble.
